Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) and “Super intelligence” (SI) are becoming a bigger and daily part of our everyday life. Companies and business use it to review job applications, banks use it to make decisions, and hospitals use it to help with healthcare. AI can save time and decision making as well as make certain tasks easier, but that does not mean Ai always gets things right.

One of the biggest concerns with Artificial intelligence and (Ai) is bias. AI systems learn from data, so if the information they are trained on contains unfair patterns or built in bias , this then can become a serious problem especially when AI is used to make decisions that affect people’s jobs, finances, education, and overall opportunities.

In this post, we will take a look at how AI bias happens, why fairness matters, and what organizations can do to prevent these problems.

How Does AI Bias Happen?

AI systems learn by looking for patterns in data. The problem is that not all data is fair or accurate or created equal. If the information used to train an AI system reflects past discrimination or inequalities, malice the system then can learn and repeat those same patterns.

Imagine a company creates an AI hiring tool then started using years of previous hiring records as its base. If most of the people hired were men, the system might start favouring male applicants, even if other applicants have the same qualifications or better.

This immediately showcases a huge problem that AI is not automatically fair just because it uses technology and mathematics. The information people provide and the decisions made in the past can influence how AI works today.

Why Fairness Matters

Fairness means making sure people are treated properly and are not put at a disadvantage because of who they are. However, treating everyone exactly the same does not always mean the outcome is fair ether.

Example, an AI hiring system might use the same scoring process for every applicant, but if it was trained using biased information, the likelihood of people that could still be treated unfairly by the ai is raised.

This matters because daily we continue to give AI more responsibilities and decisions over our lives and livelihoods. People lose their job and opportunities without even knowing a AI was involved.

I believe companies and organizations should care about more than just saving time and money. They also need to consider whether their systems and programs are actually helping people or creating more problems for the regular person.

Important AI Ethics Concepts

There are several ethics concepts that organizations should consider when developing and using AI.

  1. Fairness and Justice: AI should not unfairly disadvantage certain people or groups.
  2. Transparency: Companies should be open about when they use AI and how it is being used.
  3. Explainability: People should have a way to understand why an AI system made a particular decision.
  4. Accountability: Companies and developers should take responsibility when their AI systems make mistakes or cause harm.
  5. Privacy: Personal information should be protected and handled properly.
  6. Human Oversight: People should still be involved in important decisions instead of relying completely on AI.
  7. Beneficence: AI should be used in ways that benefit people and society.
  8. Non-Maleficence: Organizations should try to prevent their AI systems from causing harm.

I believe all these principles are important because companies need to think about how their AI systems could affect people before continuing deciding to use them.

When Amazon’s AI Hiring Tool Went Wrong

A well-known case of AI bias involved an experimental hiring tool developed by Amazon.

In 2018, Reuters reported that Amazon had created an AI system to help review job applications. The system was trained using historical hiring data, which mostly reflected applications from men.

Because of this, the AI started learning patterns that disadvantaged many female applicants. For example, it reportedly penalized some résumés that included the word “women’s” and downgraded graduates from two women’s colleges.

Amazon tried to address some of these problems, but the company eventually abandoned the project (Dastin, 2018).

I think this is a just prime example of why AI needs to be monitored. The developers did not have to directly program discrimination into the system for it to produce unfair results.

The biggest lesson I take from this example is that AI is only as reliable as the information and processes behind it.

AI Governance and Soft Ethics

AI governance is all about having rules, policies, and procedures in place that guide and dictate how AI is developed and used.

A company using AI to review job applications should have built-in safeguards or separate processes to catch bias, prevent unfair decisions, and fix problems when they arise.

However, following laws and regulations does not always mean a company is doing the right thing. This is where soft ethics comes in.

Soft ethics means looking beyond what the law requires and thinking about how decisions could affect others. For example, even if a company is legally allowed to use an AI hiring tool, it should still consider whether the system is fair to all applicants

I also believe and am a firm believer that companies should not wait until someone complains or a law forces them to make changes. They should take responsibility for their technology and think about the possible consequences before problems happen.

How Can We Reduce AI Bias?

There are a few ways we can help reduce bias in AI systems:

  • Check training data to make sure it does not contain unfair patterns.
  • Test AI systems regularly to find possible problems.
  • Have people review important decisions made with AI.
  • Explain how AI is being used and allow people to question decisions.
  • Make sure someone is responsible for fixing problems when they happen.
  • Continue monitoring systems after they are introduced.

These steps will not prevent every problem, but they will reduce the chances of AI making unfair decisions.

AI is a tool and ultimately be used to help people make quicker decisions, not completely replace human judgment. There still needs to be someone who can question the results and take responsibility when something goes wrong.

Conclusion

AI is useful in many areas, but it is still far from perfect. Bias, unfair decisions, privacy concerns, and a lack of accountability can all cause serious problems if organizations and us do not take them seriously.

The Amazon hiring tool is a just a “small” example of how AI can learn unfair patterns from historical data. Companies need to pay closer and more frequent attention to the information they use and how regularly check how their systems are performing.

Concepts such as fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, explainability, and human oversight make AI more responsible. Governance provides rules and procedures, while soft ethics encourages companies to think beyond what is legally required.

Personally, I think AI has a lot of potential, and I like what it can do, but I’m not sure how much we should trust it or the people responsible for using it. This technology is still relatively new, and we are still learning about what it can do and the problems it can create. For now, all we can really do is educate ourselves, do our research, and hope that the people developing and using AI make responsible decisions rather than using it to cause harm.

References

Dastin, J. (2018, October 10). Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women. Reuters. https://www.reuters.com/article/us-amazon-com-jobs-automation-insight/amazon-scraps-secret-ai-recruiting-tool-that-showed-bias-against-women-idUSKCN1MK08G/

Floridi, L. (2023). The ethics of artificial intelligence: Principles, challenges, and opportunities. Oxford University Press.

European Commission. (2019). Ethics guidelines for trustworthy AI. European Commission.

title: When AI Decides Your Future: The Hidden Problem of Bias

content:
Introduction

Student feedback helps colleges understand what is working and what needs improvement. It can help management decide which courses need to be updated. However, just like with great power comes ethical responsibilities.

In this situation, students must log in with their college username and password to complete a survey that claims to be anonymous. The survey then asks students to rate their instructor from 1-10, so management can use the results to decide which courses need improvement.

I think the college has a valid reason for collecting feedback, but there are many concerns about privacy that must be accounted for, trust, and fairness. Students might not feel comfortable being honest if they think their answers could be traced back to them. Instructors also deserve fair treatment and should not be judged based on one survey. The goal should be to improve courses, not blame people without understanding the full situation.

1. Ethical Issues With the Survey

My first concern is the anonymity. If students have to log in with their college accounts, how do they know their answers cannot be connected to them? Logging in does not automatically mean a survey is not anonymous, but the college needs to explain how the system works and make sure student identities are kept separate from their answers.

This relates to privacy and transparency. Students should know how their information is collected, who can access it, and how it will be used. The college should not promise anonymity unless it has checked that the system can protect it.

Another concern is the power dynamic between students and instructors. Instructors teach students and may grade their work. If students are still attending class or actively waiting for their final grades, they might worry about being penalized for giving a low rating. Even if the college has no intention of doing this, students may still feel uncomfortable sharing their real opinions.

This could affect the results because students might give higher ratings than they believe an instructor deserves just to avoid possible problems.

The rating question also has limitations. Rating an instructor from 1-10 is subjective because students can have different opinions or personal vendetta’s about the same person. A student might give a low rating because they dislike the instructor, while another might struggle because the course is difficult.

Sometimes the problem is not the instructor but the course materials, workload, or schedule. Management needs to separate these issues before deciding what needs to change. I do not think one number is enough to judge an instructor. Ratings can be useful, but they should be considered alongside written comments and other evidence. This relates to fairness and accuracy.

2. Other Ethical Issues

Removing names from survey responses does not guarantee that students cannot be identified. For example, someone might mention a specific incident or conversation in a comment. In a small class, other people might recognize who wrote it. This is called re-identification, when details can reveal someone’s identity even without their name.

Another issue is informed consent. Students should understand why the survey is being conducted, how their answers will be used, and who can see them. They should also know whether participation is voluntary or mandatory.

There is also a risk of data misuse. Management wants to improve courses, which is understandable, but it could make unfair decisions if it treats low ratings as absolutes that an instructor is doing a bad job. The results should instead be investigated instead of being used to make quick a quick judgment under haste.

Data security matters too. The college should limit access to survey responses, protect them from unauthorized access, and decide how long the information needs to be stored.

Finally, the results may not represent every student’s experience. Some students might complete the survey while others skip it because they are busy or do not trust the survey,school,management or educator. Management should remember that the responses may not tell the whole story.

3. My Recommendations to Management

My first recommendation would be to separate login verification from survey answers. The college could check that students are eligible to participate without connecting their identities to their responses.

Second, the college should clearly explain how the survey works. It should be able to tell students whether their answers are anonymous or confidential, who can access the data, and how the information will be used. Anonymous responses cannot reasonably be linked to individuals, while confidential responses may be identifiable but access is restricted.

Third, instructors should not be able to see identifiable student feedback while they are actively teaching or grading those students. Results should be reported in groups, and comments that could reveal someone’s identity should be handled carefully.

I would also recommend making participation voluntary and explaining whether choosing not to participate has any consequences. Students should not feel pressured manipulated or coerced to complete the survey or give positive feedback.

The college should improve its questions by asking separately about teaching, course materials, workload, and course design. This would help management understand what actually needs improvement instead of relying on limited information.

Numerical ratings should be considered alongside written comments and other evidence before important decisions are made. The college should also protect the data, limit access, and delete it when it is no longer needed.

Finally, management should tell students what changes were made because of their feedback. This would show that their opinions matter and help build trust between students and management.

4. What If Management Ignores My Concerns?

If management rejected my recommendations, I would explain the risks again and give clear reasons for my concerns. I would point out that students may not trust the survey if they have to log in but do not know how their identities are protected.

I would document my concerns and management’s response so there was a record of what happened. I would also suggest other ways to collect useful feedback while protecting students.

If management continued to ignore the problem, I would raise my concerns through the appropriate privacy, ethics, or management channels. I would consider the possible harm to students and instructors rather than focusing only on what management wanted.

As a data analyst, I believe I have a responsibility to be honest about the information I work with. I should not claim that a survey is anonymous if this has not been verified, or present results as more reliable than they really are.

If serious concerns remained unresolved, I would have to consider whether I could ethically continue being responsible for the work. Management may make the final decisions, but that does not mean a data analyst should ignore ethical problems. Accountability means taking responsibility for how data is collected, interpreted, and used.

Conclusion

Student surveys can help colleges improve education, but they need to be designed and used responsibly. In this situation, the main concerns are anonymity, student privacy, the power dynamic between students and instructors, and the risk of making unfair decisions based on ratings.

I think the college should explain how it collects and uses information, protect students’ identities, and look at more than one number when evaluating a course or instructor. Students need to trust the process if the college expects honest feedback, and instructors deserve a fair chance to be evaluated properly.

The biggest lesson for me is that data affects real people. Collecting information is not enough. We also need to think about how it was collected, what it actually tells us, and how it could affect others. The goal should be to use feedback to improve courses while protecting students and treating instructors fairly.
description: A look at the privacy, trust, and fairness issues in a student feedback survey that claims to be anonymous but requires a college login.
title: Anonymous or Not? The Ethics of Student Feedback Surveys
